blocks.text: Industrialization was not the sudden appearance of one machine. Energy, power, production, capital and markets began to reinforce one another. Possessing any one of these capabilities alone was insufficient for sustained industrial expansion.

Coal offered energy conditions different from those relying primarily on surface growth, while steam technology converted heat into controllable power. Machines made certain actions repeatable. Their effects depended on fuel supplies, maintenance, skills and organization.

Larger equipment and output required finance, materials and markets able to absorb products. Greater production also created demands for transport and management. Growing capability did not remove every limit; it relocated limits into new relationships and infrastructure.

The industrial threshold therefore cannot be reduced to higher efficiency. It changed work, urban concentration, investment and dependence on energy and networks. The combinations and costs through which different places crossed that threshold could still differ.
